item.title: “Greed gives rise to misfortune, Greed stirs up the mind. Greed is the inner fear Born within people. People do not recognize That special kind…
item.description:
“Greed gives rise to misfortune,
Greed stirs up the mind.
Greed is the inner fear
Born within people.
People do not recognize
That special kind of greed.

The greedy person knows not what is good,
The greedy person sees not the Dhamma.
Blindness and darkness occur
Where greed dwells together.

One who has abandoned greed,
Not greedy for what is to be craved,
For him greed falls away
Like a drop of water from a lotus leaf.

Hatred gives rise to misfortune,
Hatred stirs up the mind.
Hatred is the inner fear
Born within people.
People do not recognize
That special kind of hatred.

The hateful person knows not what is good,
The hateful person sees not the Dhamma.
Blindness and darkness occur
Where hatred dwells together.

One who has abandoned hatred,
Not hating what is hateful,
For him hatred falls away
Like a palm fruit cut from its stalk.

Delusion gives rise to misfortune,
Delusion stirs up the mind.
Delusion is the inner fear
Born within people.
People do not recognize
That special kind of delusion.

The deluded person knows not what is good,
The deluded person sees not the Dhamma.
Blindness and darkness occur
Where delusion dwells together.

One who has abandoned delusion,
Not deluded about what is delusive,
That one dispels all darkness
Like the rising sun.”

From: Itivuttaka 88

item.title: - “Venerable Sāriputta, what is happiness? What is suffering?” - “Friend, rebirth is suffering; non-rebirth is happiness. When there is rebirth, friend, this suffering is…
item.description:
- “Venerable Sāriputta, what is happiness? What is suffering?”
- “Friend, rebirth is suffering; non-rebirth is happiness. When there is rebirth, friend, this suffering is to be expected: cold, heat, hunger, thirst, defecation, urination, contact with fire, contact with a stick, contact with a sword. Even relatives and friends, when they meet and gather together, cause distress. Friend, rebirth is suffering; when there is rebirth, this suffering is to be expected. When there is no rebirth, friend, this happiness is to be expected: no cold, no heat, no hunger, no thirst, no defecation, no urination, no contact with fire, no contact with a stick, no contact with a sword. Even relatives and friends, when they meet and gather together, do not cause distress. Friend, when there is no rebirth, this happiness is to be expected.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 10.65

item.title: “Monks, there are these four noble searches. What four? Here, monks, a person being himself subject to aging, having known the peril in what is…
item.description:
“Monks, there are these four noble searches. What four? Here, monks, a person being himself subject to aging, having known the peril in what is subject to aging, seeks the unaging, supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna; being himself subject to sickness, having known the peril in sickness, seeks the unailing, supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna; being himself subject to death, having known the peril in death, seeks the deathless, supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna; being himself subject to defilement, having known the peril in defilement, seeks the undefiled, supreme security from bondage, Nibbāna. These, monks, are the four noble searches.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 4.255

item.title: “I do not see any other thing, monks, that so prevents unarisen sensual desire from arising, or abandons arisen sensual desire, as the sign of…
item.description:
“I do not see any other thing, monks, that so prevents unarisen sensual desire from arising, or abandons arisen sensual desire, as the sign of the foul. The sign of the foul, monks, when wisely attended to, prevents unarisen sensual desire from arising and abandons arisen sensual desire.”

From: Aṅguttara Nikāya 1.16

item.title: Like a great rocky mountain, Standing up to the sky, Advancing and surrounding, Crushing everything on all sides — So too, aging and death Advance…
item.description:
Like a great rocky mountain,
Standing up to the sky,
Advancing and surrounding,
Crushing everything on all sides —
So too, aging and death
Advance upon beings.
Warriors, brahmins, merchants,
Workers, outcasts,
Those who collect rubbish and feces —
No one can escape.
All are conquered.
No elephant corps,
No chariot corps, no infantry,
No battle of spells,
No battle of wealth
Can help one win
Against aging and death.
Therefore, the wise person,
Seeing what is good for oneself,
Places faith
In the Buddha, Dhamma, and Saṅgha.
Whoever by body, speech, and mind
Practices in accordance with the Dhamma,
Is praised in this life
And in the next enjoys heavenly bliss.

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 3.25

item.title: “Monks, as long as the community of monks is not dominated by craving — that craving which leads to another state of existence — then,…
item.description:
“Monks, as long as the community of monks is not dominated by craving — that craving which leads to another state of existence — then, monks, the community of monks can be expected to prosper and not decline.”

From: Dīgha Nikāya 16 – Mahāparinibbānasutta

item.title: “Monks, the bones of a single person, if collected and preserved without being destroyed, would form a heap of bones, a pile of bones, a…
item.description:
“Monks, the bones of a single person, if collected and preserved without being destroyed, would form a heap of bones, a pile of bones, a mass of bones as great as this Mount Vepulla.

The bones of a single person
Accumulated in one lifetime
Would be a heap like a mountain —
So said the Great Sage.

This great mountain of bones
Is called Vepulla,
North of Vulture’s Peak
In the Magadhan hills.

But one who sees the Four Noble Truths
With perfect wisdom —
Suffering and its origin,
The transcending of suffering,
The Noble Eightfold Path
Leading to suffering’s stilling —

That person, wandering at most
Seven more times,
Makes an end of suffering,
Destroying all fetters.”

From: Itivuttaka 24
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, knowing form as impermanent … knowing feeling as impermanent … knowing perception as impermanent … knowing formations as impermanent … knowing consciousness as impermanent,…
item.description:
“Monks, knowing form as impermanent … knowing feeling as impermanent … knowing perception as impermanent … knowing formations as impermanent … knowing consciousness as impermanent, changing, fading, ceasing — he sees all consciousness, past and present, as impermanent, suffering, subject to change. Seeing thus with correct wisdom as it actually is, all sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair are abandoned. Being abandoned, he does not become distressed. Not being distressed, he dwells at ease. Dwelling at ease, that monk is called ‘one who has stilled all signs and is wholly inclined toward Nibbāna.’”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.43
📖 Read this sutta

item.title: “Monks, what is a course of practice that is painful in the present but yields pleasant results in the future? Here, monks, a person by…
item.description:
“Monks, what is a course of practice that is painful in the present but yields pleasant results in the future? Here, monks, a person by nature has strong lust, and he constantly experiences painful and grievous feelings born of lust. By nature he has strong ill-will, and constantly experiences painful and grievous feelings born of ill-will. By nature he has strong delusion, and constantly experiences painful and grievous feelings born of delusion. With pain and grief, with tearful face and crying, he lives the holy life that is fully complete and pure. At the breakup of the body, after death, he is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world, in this realm. This, monks, is called a course of practice that is painful in the present but yields pleasant results in the future.”

From: Majjhima Nikāya 45 – Cūḷadhammasamādānasutta

item.title: “Monks, why is it called form? It is deformed (ruppati), monks, therefore it is called form. Deformed by what? Deformed by cold, deformed by heat,…
item.description:
“Monks, why is it called form? It is deformed (ruppati), monks, therefore it is called form. Deformed by what? Deformed by cold, deformed by heat, deformed by hunger, deformed by thirst, deformed by contact with flies, mosquitoes, wind, heat, and serpents. It is deformed, monks, therefore it is called form. And why, monks, is it called feeling? It feels (vedeti), monks, therefore it is called feeling. What does it feel? It feels pleasure, it feels pain, it feels neither-pain-nor-pleasure. It feels, monks, therefore it is called feeling. And why, monks, is it called perception? It perceives (sañjānāti), monks, therefore it is called perception. What does it perceive? It perceives blue, it perceives yellow, it perceives red, it perceives white. It perceives, monks, therefore it is called perception.”

From: Saṃyutta Nikāya 22.79
